851.quote_or_event: “I have totally forgotten my jealousy of others, since I found the Saadh Sangat, the Company of the Holy. … No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
851.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a mind cured of jealousy in the company of the holy: it no longer counts anyone as enemy or stranger, and it gets along with all.
851.tie_back: The Kural defines hostility as the disease that breeds the habit of not getting along with others; Guru Arjan describes the healthy opposite state, in which one gets along with everyone.
851.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
851._accuracy_note: Close inverse of the Kural's definition (getting along with all versus refusing to); the cure in Gurbani is the Saadh Sangat, and the disease image itself is not used here.

852.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists.”
852.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the seeker not to hit back at those who hit him.
852.tie_back: The Kural says that even when someone does you harm out of a wish to break with you, the best course is not to harm them in return; Farid gives the same rule of non-retaliation.
852.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 7), Bhagat Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
852._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on refusing to repay injury with injury; Farid speaks of physical blows, the Kural of any hurtful act done out of enmity.

853.quote_or_event: “Farid, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger. Your body shall not suffer from any disease, and you shall obtain everything.”
853.explanation: Farid promises that one who returns good for evil and keeps anger out of the mind will be free of disease and will gain everything.
853.tie_back: The Kural calls hostility a painful disease whose removal brings undying renown; Farid likewise ties the giving up of anger to freedom from disease and a full reward.
853.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 78), Bhagat Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
853._accuracy_note: Strong match on hostility as a disease and the gain of giving it up; Farid promises well-being and every good, not specifically the lasting fame the Kural names.

854.quote_or_event: “Do not harbor evil intentions against others in your mind, and you shall not be troubled, O Siblings of Destiny, O friends.”
854.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that whoever keeps ill will toward others out of the mind is spared trouble in his own life.
854.tie_back: The Kural says that destroying hostility, the worst of sorrows, yields the greatest joy; Guru Arjan likewise links the absence of ill will with freedom from trouble.
854.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
854._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on ill will as the source of one's own suffering; the verse promises freedom from trouble rather than the Kural's superlative joy.

855.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
855.explanation: In Japji Sahib Guru Nanak makes kinship with all people the true spiritual order and says that whoever conquers his own mind has conquered the world.
855.tie_back: The Kural asks who could ever defeat those who turn away from hostility when it rises within; Guru Nanak likewise makes victory over one's own mind, held in brotherhood with all, the victory over the world.
855.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
855._accuracy_note: Strong fit on inner self-conquest as invincibility, joined to brotherhood with all; Japji speaks of the mind in general rather than hostility specifically.

856.quote_or_event: “Do not speak ill of others, or get involved in arguments.”
856.explanation: In a chhant in Raag Vadhans Guru Nanak warns against calling others bad and stirring up quarrels.
856.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who finds it sweet to get ahead through hostility is close to ruin; Guru Nanak likewise steers the seeker away from picking quarrels.
856.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 566, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
856._accuracy_note: Next-best: it forbids the quarrelsome habit the Kural condemns, but does not state the Kural's point that delight in hostility brings ruin near.

857.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness and Dharma. Where there is falsehood, there is sin. Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
857.explanation: Kabir sets wisdom, righteousness and forgiveness against falsehood, greed and sin, placing God himself where forgiveness is.
857.tie_back: The Kural says minds bent on hostility cannot see the true principle; Kabir likewise places the truth, God himself, with forgiveness, and sin and death with its opposites.
857.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 155), Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
857._accuracy_note: Partial: forgiveness, the opposite of hostility, is where God (the true reality) dwells, but Kabir does not name hostility or say it blinds the mind.

858.quote_or_event: “Do not be angry with anyone else; look within your own self instead. Be humble in this world, O Nanak! And by His Grace you shall be carried across.”
858.explanation: In the Bavan Akhri Guru Arjan turns the seeker from anger at others to self-examination and humility, promising that grace will carry him across.
858.tie_back: The Kural says that turning away from hostility brings prosperity while pressing it on brings ruin; Guru Arjan likewise tells the seeker to turn from anger at others and promises a good end.
858.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 259, Raag Gauree, Bavan Akhri (salok before pauri 44), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
858._accuracy_note: Strong fit on turning away from anger toward others; the reward is spiritual (being carried across) rather than the worldly prosperity of the Kural.

859.quote_or_event: “Those, whom the Creator Lord would destroy - first He strips them of virtue.”
859.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak observes that those headed for destruction first lose their goodness.
859.tie_back: The Kural says that a man bringing ruin on himself looks to magnify hostility; Guru Nanak likewise reads the loss of good judgment and virtue as the first sign of coming ruin.
859.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
859._accuracy_note: Strong structural fit (moral decay as a sign of approaching ruin); Gurbani attributes it to the Creator's will (hukam), and does not single out hostility.

860.quote_or_event: “WAWWA: Do not harbor hatred against anyone. In each and every heart, God is contained. … Hatred and alienation depart from those who, as Gurmukh, listen to the Kirtan of the Lord’s Praises.”
860.explanation: Guru Arjan forbids hatred toward anyone because God lives in every heart, and says that hatred and estrangement leave those who follow the Guru and sing God's praises.
860.tie_back: The Kural closes by setting hostility, the source of every pain, against friendliness, the source of true goodness; Guru Arjan likewise roots the end of hatred and estrangement in seeing God in every heart.
860.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 259, Raag Gauree, Bavan Akhri (pauri 46), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
860._accuracy_note: Strong fit on giving up hatred and estrangement; Gurbani grounds it in God's presence in all rather than in the Kural's contrast of the fruits of hostility and friendship.
